strengths: Clean and intuitive representation: Extending 2D point map regression (as popularized by DUSt3R/MoGe) to depth-ordered layered ray intersections is an elegant, feed-forward way to perform occluded geometry reasoning without heavy volumetric grids or iterative querying.

Effective ray stopping index formulation: Formulating the valid layer mask prediction as an ordinal ray stopping index prediction naturally enforces consecutive valid surface ordering along rays, providing a substantial gain over standard independent binary mask segmentation (Table 6).

High computational efficiency: Inference requires only a single feed-forward pass (~31.5 ms for the regression model), making it significantly faster than generative 3D diffusion pipelines, NeRF queries, or multi-view hallucination methods.

Comprehensive data pipeline: The paper provides a well-reasoned data curation and coordination strategy (bridging Blender and PyTorch3D, filtering degenerate internal meshes) to enable supervision for layered ray intersections on both synthetic and real-world indoor datasets.
weaknesses: Accounting of computational footprint: The method employs two separate ViT-Large networks—one for 3D point map regression and one for ray stopping index prediction. However, Table 5 lists 314.1M parameters and 31.5 ms inference time, which corresponds only to a single ViT-Large model. The end-to-end total parameters and runtime for both models combined should be explicitly stated and compared.

Scene-level overall performance relative to visible-only baselines: In Table 2 on SCRREAM, MoGe achieves an overall FS@0.05 of 0.668 compared to 0.590 for LaRI, despite MoGe not explicitly predicting unseen surfaces. While the paper attributes this to training set scale (200K vs. 9M), this somewhat weakens the empirical claim of superior scene completion in practical evaluation.

Citation errors in the manuscript: The text incorrectly cites reference [75] (Wang et al., 2004, the SSIM paper) when referring to the ViT-Large backbone in Section 3.2 and Section 3.3, where [15] (Dosovitskiy et al.) was intended. Additionally, Table 5 cites MoGe as [73] rather than [72].

Training details on scale-shift alignment: The paper supervises point map regression via least-squares scale-shift alignment (Eq. 2–3). The text should clarify whether scale and shift parameters are detached during backpropagation (as in MiDaS/ZoeDepth) and confirm the exact per-sample batch implementation details.

strengths: The conceptual formulation of Layered Ray Intersections (LaRI) bridges single-view 2D dense prediction and complete 3D geometric reasoning in an elegant manner, enabling feed-forward unseen surface inference without slow coordinate querying or iterative diffusion sampling.

The ray stopping index regression scheme is well-motivated and structurally sound; directly enforcing the monotonic/ordinal validity along camera rays yields dramatic improvements over naive unconstrained multi-layer binary segmentation (Table 6).

The approach demonstrates remarkable efficiency and data economy: achieving competitive object reconstruction relative to heavy generative models like TRELLIS with only 4% of the training data and a fraction of the parameter count and inference time (~31 ms feed-forward).

The paper is well-structured and includes comprehensive experimental evaluation across both object-level (GSO) and scene-level (SCRREAM) domains, supported by detailed ablations on layer count, pretraining representations, and masking heads.
weaknesses: The ray intersection formulation has inherent geometric blind spots: surfaces parallel or oblique to optical rays exhibit sparse sampling density, and intricate multi-layered structures exceeding the fixed layer capacity $L$ cannot be represented without truncating geometry.

The system trains and deploys two completely separate ViT-Large networks (one for 3D intersection map regression and another for ray stopping index classification), effectively doubling model capacity and runtime; integrating them into a shared-backbone multi-task architecture is not explored.

Scene-level evaluation is relatively narrow, being conducted primarily on a subsample of 460 frames from SCRREAM; additional testing on in-the-wild images or larger amodal completion benchmarks would strengthen claims regarding generalizability.
The evaluation protocols rely heavily on scale-shift alignment (or ICP registration for canonical setups), which may partially conceal depth/scale drift and absolute metric inaccuracies.

strengths: Compelling and compact representation: Extending point map regression to layered ray intersections (LaRI) provides a neat, efficient bridge between standard 2D monocular geometry estimation and full 3D reconstruction, operating without expensive 3D queries or multi-step diffusion processes.

Effective ray stopping index formulation: Formulating the valid ray intersection identification as an ordinal ray-stopping index rather than independent per-layer binary classification naturally respects ray traversal physics, yielding significant empirical improvements (Table 6).

High computational efficiency: With an inference time of ~31.5 ms in a single feed-forward pass, LaRI is substantially faster than 3D generative baselines (e.g., TRELLIS, SPAR3D) and multi-view querying methods (e.g., CUT3R), while achieving competitive reconstruction quality.

Solid empirical results across domains: Demonstrates unified applicability across both object-level (GSO) and indoor scene-level (SCRREAM) benchmarks, outperforming baselines in view-aligned evaluation and effectively reconstructing occluded geometries.

Comprehensive data curation pipeline: Details the practical challenges of rendering layered ray intersections (e.g., handling internal mesh clutter in Objaverse, room-level mesh splitting in 3D-FRONT, and bridging Blender with PyTorch3D), providing valuable engineering insights and reproducibility commitments.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in parameter count reporting: Section 3.3 states that a separate ViT-Large backbone and dense segmentation decoder are used for predicting the ray stopping index, yet Table 5 reports 314M parameters for 'Ours' (which corresponds to a single ViT-Large encoder-decoder). The total runtime and parameter overhead of running both networks simultaneously should be clearly clarified.

Reliance on scale-shift alignment: The model predicts relative geometry supervised and evaluated via least-squares scale-shift alignment (Equations 2 and 3). While standard in monocular depth literature, this limits direct zero-shot metric deployment in physical downstream robotics tasks without external scale recovery.

Inherent geometric limitation on glancing surfaces: Because rays sample discretely along 2D pixel grids, surfaces oriented nearly parallel to the camera viewing direction suffer from severe point sparsity and ray slippage (as visible in Figure 5), which is an inherent trait of depth/intersection-based representations.

Deterministic limitation under severe occlusion: As a direct regression model, LaRI does not maintain multimodal hypotheses for heavily occluded, highly uncertain regions, which can lead to over-smoothed or collapsed average predictions in ambiguous scenes.

strengths: Clear and intuitive formulation: Formulating occluded 3D geometry reasoning as layered 3D point map regression paired with an ordinal ray-stopping index is conceptually clean, efficient, and well-motivated compared to heavy generative diffusion or iterative query-based implicit representations.

Strong empirical efficiency and performance: The feed-forward model achieves fast inference (approx. 50 ms) while achieving competitive or superior accuracy against both generative object reconstruction models (e.g., TRELLIS, SF3D, SPAR3D) and monocular depth estimators (e.g., DUSt3R, DepthPro, MoGe), particularly in unseen geometric regions.

Comprehensive dataset construction: The authors establish a systematic data generation pipeline resolving challenging coordinate convention discrepancies across Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, GSO, and SCRREAM, enabling rigorous training and evaluation for layered geometry.

Thorough ablation studies: The paper provides informative ablations covering the layer count, choice of pre-trained weights, point map versus depth map representations, ray-stopping index versus binary mask regression, and shared versus separate encoders.
weaknesses: Separate models for objects and scenes: While the representation is described as a unified recipe, the paper trains distinct models for object-level and scene-level reconstruction rather than demonstrating a single unified model that handles both domains simultaneously.

Inherent geometric limitation of ray casting: As acknowledged by the authors, surfaces parallel to viewing rays or complex concave geometries behind occlusions suffer from sparse point density and incomplete reconstruction due to the fixed viewing grid.

Relative geometry and scale ambiguity: Because the supervision and evaluation rely on least-squares scale-shift alignment, the predicted point maps do not provide true metric depth/scale, limiting direct deployment in metric downstream robotics applications without additional sensor calibration or alignment.

Citation error: In Section 3.2, ViT-Large is erroneously cited as (Wang et al., 2004), which corresponds to the SSIM image quality assessment paper rather than the Vision Transformer work (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020).

strengths: The paper introduces a clean, feed-forward formulation for single-view occluded geometry reasoning by predicting layered 3D point maps (LaRI), effectively bridging the gap between visible-only depth/point-map estimators and slow generative/query-based representations.

The ray stopping index regression formulation (Eq. 6-7) is elegant and well-motivated; it naturally enforces the physical constraint of contiguous surface intersections along a ray, outperforming unconstrained multi-layer binary segmentation by a substantial margin (Table 7).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering both object-level (GSO) and indoor scene-level (3D-FRONT, SCRREAM) benchmarks under canonical and view-aligned settings, with thorough ablations on layer count, pre-trained visual representations, per-layer error progression, and point map vs. depth map representations.

Significant inference speed advantages over existing generative and query-based complete 3D reconstruction models (e.g., ~14-17x faster than TRELLIS and SPAR3D) while maintaining competitive or superior geometry fidelity.
weaknesses: The method requires two separate ViT-Large backbones (one for point map regression and one for stopping index prediction, totaling ~620M parameters) because sharing the encoder causes noticeable performance drops (Table 8). This increases the memory footprint and limits deployment on edge devices.

The object-level and scene-level models are trained separately on different datasets (Objaverse vs. 3D-FRONT/ScanNet++), rather than demonstrating a single unified foundation model capable of handling arbitrary inputs.

Predictions are supervised and evaluated using scale-shift alignment (Eq. 4), meaning the model only predicts relative geometry rather than metric scale, which limits its direct plug-and-play utility in downstream robotics and spatial computing pipelines without external scale estimation.

As an inherent limitation of ray-intersection representations, surfaces roughly parallel to camera rays suffer from low point sampling density, and the paper does not demonstrate mesh surface extraction from the resulting multi-layer point sets.

strengths: Principled and practical formulation: Adapting the classical computer graphics concept of Layered Depth Images (LDIs) into a feed-forward multi-layer 3D point map regression framework offers a compelling alternative to computationally heavy generative diffusion models, NeRF-based sampling, or multi-view query heuristics for occluded geometry reasoning.

Effective ray-stopping index mechanism: Formulating the validity of ray intersections as an ordinal stopping-index classification problem rather than unconstrained binary multi-label segmentation naturally enforces the physical constraint of ray propagation. The ablation in Table 7 empirically validates this choice with massive gains over binary segmentation (e.g., mIoU from 0.091 to 0.560 on GSO).

Comprehensive dataset curation effort: The authors develop an extensive annotation and rendering pipeline utilizing PyTorch3D and Blender across five diverse datasets (Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, SCRREAM, and GSO), carefully addressing coordinate frame discrepancies and internal mesh artifacts.

Strong efficiency and solid empirical validation: LaRI demonstrates substantial inference speed advantages over generative 3D reconstruction models (e.g., ~51.5 ms vs. 733.7 ms for TRELLIS and 904.8 ms for SPAR3D) while maintaining competitive accuracy, and establishes clear quantitative advantages in recovering unseen surface regions compared to existing single-view feed-forward baselines.

Extensive ablation studies: The appendix and main text thoroughly analyze critical design decisions, including the layer budget $L$, pre-trained initialization priors (DINO-v2/v3 vs. geometric priors), point-map vs. depth parameterizations, per-layer error distributions, and shared vs. separate encoders.
weaknesses: Dual-network architecture requirement: The pipeline relies on two separate ViT-Large backbones—one for point-map regression and one for ray-stopping index prediction—totaling over 620M parameters. As demonstrated in Table 8, attempting to share an encoder leads to non-negligible performance drops, which undermines the architectural elegance and doubles the backbone computational footprint.

Lack of cross-domain model unification: Despite presenting LaRI as a unified recipe for both object-level and scene-level geometry, the object model (trained on Objaverse) and scene model (trained on 3D-FRONT and ScanNet++) are trained and evaluated completely separately (Section 4.1), meaning the representations and learned priors have not yet been demonstrated to generalize within a single unified network checkpoint.

Inherent geometric sampling bias along ray directions: Representing 3D geometry via discrete ray intersections causes noticeable point sparsity on surfaces nearly parallel to viewing rays (grazing angles) and cannot capture complex lateral geometries that camera rays do not cross, as acknowledged in Figure 5.

Dependence on scale-shift alignment: The network predicts relative coordinate maps up to an unknown global scale and z-shift, requiring post-hoc least-squares scale-shift alignment (Eq. 4) against ground truth during evaluation, leaving absolute/metric scale recovery unaddressed for monocular inference.

Citation inaccuracy: In Section 3.2 (page 4) and Section 3.3 (page 5), the ViT-Large backbone is erroneously cited as `(Wang et al., 2004)` (which corresponds to the SSIM image quality metric paper in the reference list) rather than Dosovitskiy et al. (2020).
